title: Check yourself: Permissions that bound the tools, exploring a codebase and the practice

questions.stem: A repository's settings deny `Read(./.env)`. The agent, trying to fix a bug, calls Edit on `.env`. What happens?

options.text: It is refused, as the rule reaches the tools that write there
options.says: A read denial covers the tools that change content at the same path.

options.text: It proceeds, since only reading calls are matched by that rule
options.says: Ruled out because "A `Read(...)` deny rule also blocks the Edit and Write tools on the same path, including creating a new file there".

options.text: A person is asked, since no edit rule names that path
options.says: Ruled out because a deny is checked before anything else: "Deny is checked before ask and allow".

options.text: It proceeds, since the working directory counts as trusted
options.says: Ruled out because "If a deny rule matches, the tool is blocked, even in `bypassPermissions` mode."

questions.stem: A team's audit hook has the matcher `Grep` and logs nothing in a default Linux session, though the agent searches constantly. What explains it?

options.text: Hook matchers apply only to tools that come from MCP servers
options.says: Ruled out because the tool names are "the exact strings you use in permission rules, subagent tool lists, and hook matchers".

options.text: Hooks cannot observe the search tools on any platform
options.says: Ruled out because "the searches reach your hooks and permission rules as `Bash` calls".

options.text: Its lookups run through the shell tool, so only a Bash entry sees them
options.says: On macOS, Linux and WSL the default set has no Grep, and its job is done through the shell tool.

options.text: A matcher takes the parenthesised rule form, so a bare tool name never fires
options.says: Ruled out because "Hook `matcher` fields use bare tool names, not the parenthesized rule format."
